anchor.surface_text: 10.  During the 1930s he acquired for value a two-floor freestone building, constructed in 1906, in the sub-prefecture of Tarsus, İçel province. The building, which had a total floor space of 516.34 m², was of architectural interest in its own right.

facts.text: On 1 November 1990 the Committee for the Protection of Adana's Cultural and Natural Heritage classified the property as a “cultural asset” under the Cultural and Natural Heritage (Protection) Act.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  On 1 November 1990 the Committee for the Protection of Adana's Cultural and Natural Heritage decided to classify the property as a “cultural asset” within the meaning of the Cultural and Natural Heritage (Protection) Act (Law no. 2863 of 21 July 1983).

facts.text: On 23 November 1998 the building was included in the project for protection of the urban environment and also on the Council of Europe's inventory for protection of cultural and natural heritage.

anchor.surface_text: On 23 November 1998 it was included in the project for protection of the urban environment. It was also included on the Council of Europe's inventory for the protection of the cultural and natural heritage.

facts.text: On 4 April 2000 the executive council of İçel province issued an expropriation order for the property as part of the Project for environmental rehabilitation and regeneration of streets around St Paul's Well.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  On 4 April 2000 the executive council of İçel province issued an expropriation order in respect of the property in the context of the “Project for the environmental rehabilitation and regeneration of the streets around St Paul's Well”.

facts.text: A valuation report by a panel of experts on 21 March 2000 valued the building at 36,856,865,000 Turkish liras (about 65,326 euros), which was paid to the applicant on transfer of ownership.

anchor.surface_text: On the basis of a valuation report submitted on 21 March 2000 by a panel of experts (hereafter “panel no. 1”) made up of three representatives of the authorities and two representatives of property owners, and in line with the “high-grade building” category in the construction price index published by the Ministry of Urban Planning, the council determined the building's value at 36,856,865,000 Turkish liras (TRL) (about 65,326 euros (EUR)[1]). This amount was paid to the applicant on the date of transfer of ownership.

facts.text: On 12 October 2000 the applicant applied to the Tarsus District Court for increased compensation, requesting a new expert panel including a qualified art historian to reassess the property considering its historical and architectural value, claiming 1,000,000,000,000 TRL (about 1,728,750 euros) additional compensation.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  On 12 October 2000 the applicant lodged an application for increased compensation for the expropriated building with the Tarsus District Court. He requested that a new panel of experts, to include a qualified art historian, re-assess the property, taking into account its historical and architectural value. He claimed TRL 1,000,000,000,000 (about EUR 1,728,750) in additional compensation.

facts.text: On 26 February 2001 the court dismissed the applicant's request for re-valuation based on historical value but agreed to appoint a new panel of experts including a civil engineer, architect, and property owner representative.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 26 February 2001 the court held a hearing and dismissed the applicant's request for re-valuation of the building on the ground of its historical value. The court held, inter alia, that under section 11 (1) of the Expropriation Act (Law no. 2942) (see paragraph 29 below), the panel of experts responsible for the building's valuation could only determine its value on the basis of clearly defined objective data. At the same time, it agreed to the appointment of a new panel of experts, to be made up of a civil engineer, an architect and a representative of property owners.

facts.text: On 10 May 2001, the court-appointed panel of experts (panel no. 2) submitted a report describing the property's location, historical and cultural significance, architectural features, and assessed its value based on construction price index for buildings requiring restoration, applying a 50% depreciation rate.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  On 10 May 2001, after visiting the site, the court-appointed panel of experts (hereafter panel no. 2) submitted its report. With regard to those features and factors which had a bearing on the property's value, it reached the following conclusions: “The property in question is located in the Camicedit neighbourhood, within the territory of Tarsus, in the Mersin District. It is recorded in the land register as a solid structure house with a courtyard. Situated in an urban area, it is classed as a listed building in the project for protection of the urban heritage. The decision to classify the building was adopted by the Committee for the Protection of Adana's Cultural and Natural Heritage on 1 November 1990...

facts.text: Panel no. 2 concluded that panel no. 1 had valued the building as an ordinary dressed-stone building without considering architectural features, and assessed the building's value initially at 181,448,588,000 TRL, applying a 50% depreciation but then increasing the value by 100% due to architectural, historical, and cultural features, resulting in additional compensation of 144,591,723,000 TRL.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  Panel no. 2 concluded that panel no. 1 (see paragraph 12 above) had valued the disputed building as an ordinary dressed-stone building, without taking account of its architectural features. It decided not to adopt those valuation criteria and assessed the building's value at an initial TRL 181,448,588,000. It then reduced this amount to TRL 90,724,294,000, noting that the building's depreciation justified a reduction of 50%. However, it then increased this sum to TRL 181,448,588,000, holding that, in view of the building's architectural, historical and cultural features, its value should be increased by 100 %. After deduction of the expropriation compensation already paid to the applicant, the panel decided that the additional compensation should be TRL 144,591,723,000.

facts.text: A third panel of experts (panel no. 3) submitted a report on 12 June 2001 confirming the conclusions of panel no. 2's report.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  A third panel of experts (hereafter “panel no. 3”) submitted a report on 12 June 2001, confirming all of the conclusions in the second expert report.

facts.text: On 14 June 2001 the applicant requested a further expert report, arguing the previous reports failed to sufficiently consider the building's architectural and historical features.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  On 14 June 2001 the applicant requested a further expert report, on the ground that the two previous reports had failed to take sufficient account of the building's architectural and historical features in assessing its value.

facts.text: On 15 June 2001 the court dismissed the request for an additional expert report but allowed part of the applicant's claim, instructing payment of 144,591,723,000 TRL in additional compensation with interest from 3 October 2000.

anchor.surface_text: 20.  On 15 June 2001 the court, after dismissing the request for an additional expert report, allowed part of the applicant's claim and instructed the authorities to pay him TRL 144,591,723,000 (about EUR 139,728) in additional compensation, with interest at the statutory rate, to be calculated from 3 October 2000.

facts.text: On 19 November 2001 the Court of Cassation set aside the district court's judgment, holding that under section 15(d) of the Cultural and Natural Heritage Act, architectural or historical features or rarity could not be considered in assessing value, thus a 100% increase was unjustified.

anchor.surface_text: 21.  On 19 November 2001 the Court of Cassation set aside that judgment. It held that under section 15 (d) of the Cultural and Natural Heritage (Protection) Act (Law no. 2863), neither a building's architectural or historical features nor those resulting from its rarity could enter into play in the assessment of its value. Consequently, a 100 % increase in the amount of additional compensation could not be considered justified.

facts.text: On 4 December 2001 the applicant petitioned for rectification of the Court of Cassation's judgment, contesting the amount of compensation and the absence of legal criteria for valuing cultural and historical heritage buildings, relying on Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  On 4 December 2001 the applicant petitioned for rectification of the Court of Cassation's judgment. arguments.claim: The Government contended that the building was State property as part of the common heritage and owners had limited rights only to the land, not the building's cultural/artistic value.

anchor.surface_text: The Government specified that under the Cultural and Natural Heritage (Protection) Act (Law no. 2863 of 21 July 1983) buildings of cultural or artistic interest which belonged to individuals were considered to be State property, in the same way as those that belonged to public establishments, on the ground that they were part of the population's common heritage. Consequently, their owners had only limited property rights over them, in the sense that such rights applied only to the land on which the buildings were situated.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the public interest in protecting cultural heritage but found the compensation system unfair as it excluded value arising from architectural and historical features.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the building's value would have diminished due to its classification as protected property, obliging the owner to sell at a lower price if not expropriated.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that the building in question, which was located in a classified zone, had been expropriated in the context of the “Project for the environmental rehabilitation and regeneration of the streets around St Paul's Well”. They alleged that even if the authorities had not expropriated it, its value would have diminished considerably on account of its classification as a protected property. The applicant would thus have been obliged to sell it at a price significantly lower than the amount received in compensation for the expropriation.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court acknowledged valuation difficulties but held these do not justify ignoring architectural and historical features in compensation.

arguments.claim: The Government maintained that the compensation awarded by domestic courts was reasonably related to the value of the expropriated property, considering its historical/artistic features as part of common heritage.

anchor.surface_text: In conclusion, the Government considered that, having regard to the margin of appreciation left by Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the national authorities, the compensation awarded by the domestic courts had been reasonably related to the value of the expropriated property, which, on account of its historical and/or artistic features, was, they argued, part of the common heritage.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the valuation system unfair and disproportionate as it excluded value from architectural and historical features.

arguments.claim: The applicant claimed pecuniary damage based on expert reports indicating the building's architectural features justified a 100% increase in value, and argued for a 400% increase.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant claimed 1,392,000 US dollars (USD) (the equivalent of TRL 907,242,940,000 under the exchange rate at the relevant time) in respect of pecuniary damage. He pointed out that, according to the experts, the building's architectural features justified a 100% increase in its value, which should thus be set at TRL 181,448,588,000, without taking into account the property's age. In his opinion, the historical, artistic and cultural value of his building would in reality justify an increase of about 400%. Thus, in his submission, the sum of TRL 181,448,588,000 should be multiplied by five in order to establish the pecuniary damage he had sustained.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court noted the applicant's valuation method was not based on objective data or expert support and could not be accepted.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court rejected the Government's argument that the compensation including land and interest represented fair compensation, emphasizing the need to consider the building's specific features.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the compensation awarded was insufficient as it failed to reflect the property's architectural and historical value.

outcome.relief_summary: The Court found a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and awarded the applicant EUR 75,000 for pecuniary damage and EUR 1,000 for costs and expenses, plus interest. The finding of a violation was considered sufficient just satisfaction for non-pecuniary damage. The remainder of the applicant's claim for just satisfaction was dismissed.
directions: The respondent State is to pay the awarded sums within three months, converted into Turkish liras at the applicable rate on the date of settlement.
Simple interest is payable on the awarded amounts from the expiry of the three months until settlement at the ECB marginal lending rate plus three percentage points.
